title: Act I, Scene III
focus: Juliet, her mother and the Nurse

teacherSummary.text: Lady Capulet calls Juliet to discuss marriage; the Nurse interrupts with a long, bawdy story of Juliet's weaning and her late husband's joke. Lady Capulet describes Paris as a fine book that needs only a cover and asks if Juliet can love him. Juliet agrees to look at him, but no more than her mother allows.

context.history: Wealthy families commonly employed a wet-nurse to breastfeed infants; the Nurse lost her own daughter, Susan, and nursed Juliet. The 'earthquake' she mentions has been linked by some scholars to a 1580 English earthquake.

significance: The scene introduces the Nurse as Juliet's real confidante and Lady Capulet as distant; Juliet's careful answer shows her before love changes her.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Juliet is not yet fourteen, and her mother and the Nurse press her toward marriage; the Nurse's jokes are bawdy. Name the age openly, set it against Elizabethan norms (most English brides were in their twenties), and discuss consent and family pressure critically.
contentNotes.studentPreview: This scene discusses marrying off a thirteen-year-old and includes crude jokes.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “How does Juliet answer her mother, and what does that show about her choices?”
